analysis.one_liner: Ends the farmworker exemption from overtime pay and phases in time-and-a-half after a standard workweek.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote after being referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to end the special rule that has excluded farmworkers from overtime pay since 1938. Employers would owe time-and-a-half after 55 hours a week in 2019, stepping down to 40 hours by 2022, with later start dates for farms with 25 or fewer employees. It would also strike overtime exemptions for related industries such as cotton ginning and sugar processing.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly two million farmworkers and workers in agriculture-related jobs would gain a right most other American workers already have: time-and-a-half pay after a standard workweek. The benefit would phase in over several years, reaching a 40-hour threshold by 2022 for most employers and 2025 for the smallest ones.

how_it_helps.text: Grants agricultural workers time-and-a-half pay for hours above a standard workweek, phasing the threshold down from 55 hours in 2019 to 40 hours in 2022 for most employers.
Repeals the section of the 1938 law (subsection 7(m)) that has excluded farmworkers from overtime pay, ending a nearly 80-year carve-out from protections other workers receive.

Removes overtime exemptions for workers in agriculture-related industries, including small farms' exemptions beyond immediate family, cotton ginning and compressing, sugar processing, and irrigation projects.
Gives employers with 25 or fewer employees a longer runway: overtime requirements would not start for them until 2022, with the full 40-hour threshold reached by 2025.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural employers, especially larger farms and agriculture-related businesses like cotton gins and sugar processors, would pay overtime wages for hours above the standard workweek. Small farms with 25 or fewer employees would get more time to adjust, but would eventually bear the same costs, which could be passed on in food prices or absorbed as reduced hours.

drawbacks.text: The bill would raise labor costs for agricultural employers, and small farms in particular operate on thin margins; the bill acknowledges this by delaying the requirements for employers with 25 or fewer workers until 2022-2025.
Higher overtime costs could lead some employers to cap workers' hours below the new threshold or shift to piece rates, reducing take-home pay for workers who rely on long hours during harvest season.
Costs could be passed to consumers through higher food prices, though the multi-year phase-in limits the immediate impact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large for the workers affected: farmworkers are among the lowest-paid workers in the country, and they have been excluded from overtime pay since 1938 while nearly all other workers gained it. The costs fall on employers, some of them genuinely small farms, and could mean fewer hours or higher food prices; the bill's long phase-in and small-employer delay are designed to soften that, but they also mean the smallest operations face the change last and the full 40-hour threshold would not arrive for most employers until 2022 or later. The bill is a straightforward extension of an existing standard rather than a novel policy, which weighs in its favor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2018 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no hearing or vote, and the full House never considered the bill before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
All 65 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; the committee that would have considered it was chaired by a Republican, Virginia Foxx.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers are better off because the bill died: farmworkers remain exempt from overtime pay, so no added wage costs take effect. Farmworkers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva

for.name: 65 of 235 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and senior committee members; it received no other chamber action.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the majority and never brought the bill to the House floor; it never received a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported it; the bill died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (farms, ranches, and farm labor contractors)
industries.note: Farms and agricultural businesses have long paid no overtime to farmworkers under a 1938 exemption, so extending overtime raises their labor costs directly. The bill never advanced, so that cost never arrived.

industries.industry: Agriculture-related processors (cotton ginning, sugar processing, irrigation projects)
industries.note: The bill repeals specific overtime exemptions for these agriculture-related employers, exposing them to the same time-and-a-half requirement as other covered businesses.
